items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; antipsychotics/clonidine/dexmedetomidine adjuncts only, without seizure protection

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure

table.title: Approximate onset after reduction; overlap common

appendicitis.name: Appendicitis
appendicitis.scope: Acute appendicitis, clinical presentation, pediatric and pregnancy considerations, imaging (ultrasound, CT), surgical management
appendicitis.core: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, followed by anorexia and nausea, suggests appendiceal inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescents/young adults; luminal obstruction by lymphoid hyperplasia or fecalith
Older adults may have obstructing neoplasm; immunosuppression can blunt findings

rows.label: Clues
items: McBurney tenderness, guarding, fever; Rovsing, psoas, or obturator signs depend on position
★ **Diffuse peritonitis, toxicity, hypotension** → perforation/sepsis until proven otherwise
Young children: nonspecific symptoms and rapid progression; pregnancy: displaced appendix, less reliable examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal obstruction → distention, venous congestion, bacterial invasion → ischemia/perforation
Visceral midgut pain precedes focal parietal peritoneal irritation

rows.label: Dx
items: CBC, urinalysis, **pregnancy test** in reproductive-age patients; pyuria does not exclude appendicitis
★ Stable nonpregnant adult → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** when diagnosis uncertain
★ Child/pregnancy → **ultrasound first**; nondiagnostic → MRI without gadolinium, or CT in nonpregnant child
Noncompressible enlarged appendix >6 mm with periappendiceal inflammation supports diagnosis
Clear peritonitis → surgical evaluation; do not delay necessary operation for repeated imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ NPO, **IV fluids, analgesia, ceftriaxone + metronidazole**, surgical consultation
Laparoscopic appendectomy definitive; do not withhold necessary surgery during pregnancy
Selected uncomplicated cases → antibiotics after shared decision; recurrence/failure higher, especially with appendicolith
Localized abscess/phlegmon in stable patient → antibiotics ± image-guided drainage; follow-up based on age/risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Perforation, abscess, peritonitis, sepsis, ileus
Postoperative wound infection, intra-abdominal collection, adhesional obstruction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, adnexal findings
Ovarian torsion: sudden unilateral pelvic pain; gastroenteritis: diarrhea prominent before diffuse cramping
Mesenteric adenitis: viral prodrome, normal appendix on imaging

appendicitis.evidence: Not checked online; established general-surgery evaluation and treatment principles.

atrial-fibrillation.name: Atrial fibrillation
atrial-fibrillation.scope: Rate and rhythm control, stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc), unstable AF, embolic complications
atrial-fibrillation.core: Disorganized atrial activation produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm and left atrial appendage thromboembolism risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, hypertension, heart failure, coronary disease, obesity, sleep apnea
Hyperthyroidism, alcohol binges, infection, postoperative stress, mitral valve disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Palpitations, exercise intolerance, dyspnea; sometimes incidental or first detected after stroke
★ **Hypotension, ischemic chest pain, pulmonary edema, altered mentation** → unstable AF
Very rapid irregular wide-complex rhythm suggests preexcitation; ordinary AV nodal blockers can be dangerous

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pulmonary-vein ectopic triggers plus atrial remodeling sustain reentry
Loss of atrial contraction reduces filling; persistent tachycardia can impair LV function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG: absent discrete P waves**, variable RR intervals; document rhythm rather than pulse alone
TSH, electrolytes, renal function; transthoracic echocardiogram for ventricular function and structural disease
Intermittent symptoms → ambulatory rhythm monitoring; assess reversible triggers

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → **synchronized cardioversion**; do not delay for anticoagulation or TEE
Stable rate control: metoprolol or diltiazem; avoid diltiazem/verapamil with reduced EF
Decompensated HF: digoxin or amiodarone; preexcited AF: procainamide or cardioversion, no AV nodal blockers
Rhythm control for symptoms, early disease, or HF: cardioversion, selected antiarrhythmics, catheter ablation
★ Duration ≥48 hours/unknown: **3 weeks anticoagulation or TEE** before elective cardioversion; ≥4 weeks afterward

rows.label: Complications
items: Systemic emboli to brain, mesentery, limbs; tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
Anticoagulant bleeding; rhythm drugs may cause proarrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Long-term anticoagulation: **CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 men/≥3 women**; consider one point lower
Apixaban/other DOAC preferred; mechanical valve or moderate/severe rheumatic mitral stenosis → warfarin
Weight reduction, BP/OSA treatment, limit alcohol; aspirin does not substitute for anticoagulation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atrial flutter: sawtooth atrial activity, often regular 2:1 conduction
Multifocal atrial tachycardia: ≥3 P-wave morphologies, isoelectric intervals

burn-injuries.name: Burn injuries
burn-injuries.scope: Superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness burns, total body surface area (Rule of Nines), fluid resuscitation (Parkland), smoke inhalation and airway edema, carbon monoxide/cyanide toxicity
burn-injuries.core: Burn severity depends on depth, affected surface area, location, and inhalation injury; airway threats and hypovolemia take priority over wound care.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Flames/scalds, electricity, chemicals; closed-space fires increase toxic inhalation risk
Older adults, children, impaired mobility/sensation; inconsistent injury history raises abuse concern

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hoarseness, stridor, oropharyngeal edema, soot** → threatened airway; skin burns may appear minor
CO: headache, confusion, syncope despite normal pulse oximetry
Cyanide: enclosed-fire exposure with cardiovascular collapse and severe lactic acidosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Capillary leak → intravascular depletion and edema; swelling progresses after initial presentation
CO impairs oxygen transport; cyanide blocks mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TBSA excludes superficial burns**; adult Rule of Nines: head/each arm 9%, each leg 18%
Anterior/posterior trunk 18% each, perineum 1%; own palm including fingers ≈1%; children → Lund-Browder
★ Inhalation/toxin concern → **ABG with co-oximetry**, lactate; normal PaO2 does not exclude CO
Electrical burn → ECG, CK, urinalysis for rhabdomyolysis; small surface injury may hide deep damage

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway threat → **intubate**; burn center: full-thickness, ≥10% partial, critical-site, inhalation/electrical/chemical
CO → 100% oxygen; severe neurologic/cardiac toxicity or pregnancy → consider hyperbaric oxygen; cyanide → hydroxocobalamin
Lactated Ringer: classic **Parkland = 4 mL × kg × %TBSA** during first 24 hours
Half by 8 hours from injury, remainder over 16; ABA now starts adults at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA

rows.label: Complications
items: Shock, AKI, infection, contractures, compartment syndrome; overresuscitation worsens edema
Restrictive chest/limb eschar → escharotomy; true compartment syndrome → fasciotomy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Titrate fluids to urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults; formula only starting estimate
Analgesia, cleaning, moist nonadherent dressings, tetanus; avoid routine systemic antibiotic prophylaxis
★ **Stop exposure, remove jewelry, cool water**, prevent hypothermia; no ice
Smoke/CO detectors, safe water temperature, fire escape plan; early rehabilitation and range of motion

rows.label: Mimics
items: SJS/TEN: medication exposure, mucosal erosions, widespread epidermal detachment
Cellulitis: spreading warmth/erythema without immediate thermal exposure

table.title: Depth
rows: Moist blisters, brisk blanching, very painful

burn-injuries.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ABA burn resuscitation guideline 2024](https://academic.oup.com/jbcr/article/45/3/565/7458089); classic Parkland contrasted with current initial estimate.

cervicitis-pid.name: Cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease
cervicitis-pid.core: Sexually active patient with mucopurulent discharge or postcoital bleeding; ascending infection adds pelvic pain, sometimes an adnexal abscess.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <25, new/multiple partners, inconsistent condoms, prior STI
IUD-associated PID risk concentrated within first 3 weeks after insertion

rows.label: Clues
items: Cervical friability, easily induced endocervical bleeding; infection sometimes asymptomatic
Dyspareunia, fever; severe unilateral pain/adnexal mass → **tubo-ovarian abscess**
Peritonitis, shock → rupture; RUQ pain → Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GC/CT ascend cervix → endometrium/tubes; PID often polymicrobial, including anaerobes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test** first; vaginal/cervical or urine **GC/CT NAAT**; HIV/syphilis testing
★ Pelvic pain + **cervical motion, uterine, OR adnexal tenderness** → presumptive PID; no confirmation delay
Negative cervical NAAT does not exclude upper-tract infection; normal discharge/no vaginal leukocytes argues against PID
**Transvaginal US** for abscess or diagnostic uncertainty; routine laparoscopy unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Cervicitis: empiric GC/CT coverage IF high risk/unreliable follow-up; otherwise await NAAT
★ Admit IF **pregnant, abscess, severe illness**, oral intolerance, uncertain surgical diagnosis, or failure by 72 h
Abscess rupture → emergency surgery; persistent abscess after 48–72 h antibiotics → drainage
Pregnant chlamydia → **azithromycin**, avoid doxycycline; retain IUD initially, reassess if no improvement

rows.label: Complications
items: Tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain; abscess → sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from prior **60 days**; abstain until courses completed, partners treated, symptoms resolved
Retest GC/CT at 3 months; pregnant chlamydia → test of cure at 4 weeks
Annual GC/CT screening: sexually active women <25, older women with risks; condoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, no confirmed intrauterine pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt unilateral pain, vomiting; Doppler flow may persist
Appendicitis: migrating RLQ pain, CT appendiceal inflammation

table.title: Antibiotic branches
rows: Ceftriaxone; add CT regimen unless excluded
Oral drugs 14 days; ceftriaxone once IM outpatient

copd.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
copd.scope: Stable COPD, acute exacerbation (AECOPD), oxygen-induced hypercapnia, noninvasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP), indications for intubation, bronchodilators and glucocorticoids
copd.core: Persistent airflow obstruction after inhalational exposure causes progressive exertional dyspnea and episodic infectious or inflammatory exacerbations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Tobacco, biomass smoke, occupational dusts; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with early/basilar emphysema

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic cough/sputum, prolonged expiration, wheeze, hyperinflation
★ **Somnolence, exhaustion, silent chest, worsening acidosis** → impending respiratory failure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Small-airway inflammation + alveolar destruction → expiratory collapse, air trapping, impaired diffusion
Excess oxygen worsens CO₂ retention mainly through V/Q mismatch and Haldane effect

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Postbronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.70** confirms persistent obstruction in compatible clinical setting
Exacerbation: pulse oximetry; ABG for severe distress/altered mentation; radiograph for pneumonia, edema, pneumothorax
Consider ECG, troponin, BNP, or PE evaluation when symptoms exceed expected exacerbation pattern

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **albuterol + ipratropium**, prednisone for 5 days; titrate oxygen to 88–92%
Antibiotics: purulence + increased dyspnea/sputum volume, or ventilatory support; doxycycline/azithromycin options
★ Hypercapnic acidosis, pH ≤7.35 → **BiPAP** unless aspiration risk, arrest, instability, inability to cooperate
Intubate for failed NIV, severe encephalopathy, refractory hypoxemia, or inability to protect airway
Long-term oxygen if stable PaO₂ ≤55 or saturation ≤88%; selected cor pulmonale/polycythemia with PaO₂ 56–59

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, secondary polycythemia, cachexia
Pneumonia risk with inhaled steroids; ventilation → dynamic hyperinflation, auto-PEEP, barotrauma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Smoking cessation**, influenza/COVID/pneumococcal/RSV vaccination when eligible, pulmonary rehabilitation
Check inhaler technique/adherence; offer alpha-1 antitrypsin testing at least once

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: variable symptoms and reversible obstruction
Heart failure: orthopnea, edema, vascular congestion; bronchiectasis: copious sputum, dilated bronchi

table.title: Stable inhaled treatment
rows: Exacerbations with eosinophilia or concurrent asthma

copd.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [GOLD 2026](https://goldcopd.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/GOLD-REPORT-2026-v1.3-8Dec2025_WMV2.pdf); acute ventilatory care: established teaching.

drowning-and-submersion-injury.name: Drowning and submersion injury
drowning-and-submersion-injury.scope: Submersion injury, nonfatal drowning, hypoxemia, acute lung injury/ARDS, electrolyte disturbances, observation criteria
drowning-and-submersion-injury.core: Respiratory impairment from submersion causes hypoxemia; prompt ventilation is the central lifesaving intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unsupervised children, absent barriers/life jackets, alcohol, seizures, syncope, risky water activity
Cold water, prolonged submersion, delayed rescue, underlying cardiac channelopathy worsen risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Cough, dyspnea, crackles, frothy sputum, hypothermia, altered consciousness
★ **Persistent hypoxemia or respiratory distress** predicts evolving lung injury despite initially mild examination
Freshwater versus saltwater rarely changes clinical management or causes meaningful systemic electrolyte shifts

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Aspiration washes out surfactant and injures alveoli → noncardiogenic edema, intrapulmonary shunt
Systemic oxygen deprivation causes bradycardia, cardiac arrest, and neurologic injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Assess **oxygenation, breathing, temperature, mental status** immediately
ABG/electrolytes for severe injury; chest radiograph for respiratory symptoms, not mandatory in completely well patients
Evaluate trauma, intoxication, arrhythmia, seizure, or hypoglycemia as precipitating cause
Early normal radiograph does not guarantee normal subsequent respiratory course

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Safe rescue → **rescue breaths plus CPR** if arrest; oxygen/BVM for inadequate respirations
Intubate for refractory hypoxemia, severe fatigue, or absent airway protection; lung-protective ventilation with PEEP
Remove wet clothing, rewarm; immobilize cervical spine only when mechanism suggests injury
★ No routine **antibiotics or corticosteroids**; antibiotics for infection or grossly contaminated-water exposure
Observe mild cases 4–6 hours; admit for abnormal mentation, oxygen requirement, persistent symptoms, or deterioration

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, hypoxic brain injury, pneumonia, arrhythmia, multiorgan dysfunction
Pulmonary edema may evolve over hours; asymptomatic wellness for days does not predict sudden delayed drowning

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Four-sided pool fencing**, touch supervision, swim lessons, properly fitted life jackets
Avoid alcohol and swimming alone; seizure precautions; caregivers trained in ventilation-inclusive CPR

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiogenic edema: primary cardiac disease, elevated filling pressures
Immersion pulmonary edema: swimming-associated dyspnea without submersion/aspiration
Aspiration pneumonitis: gastric contents after vomiting rather than water exposure

ectopic-pregnancy.name: Ectopic pregnancy
ectopic-pregnancy.scope: Diagnosis (beta-hCG, transvaginal ultrasound, discriminatory zone), unruptured ectopic pregnancy, medical management (methotrexate), ruptured ectopic pregnancy, surgical management
ectopic-pregnancy.core: Pregnancy implanted outside the endometrial cavity, usually tubal; early pregnancy with pelvic pain or bleeding requires localization and rupture assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior ectopic, PID/tubal damage, tubal surgery, infertility treatment, smoking
IUDs prevent pregnancy overall; pregnancy despite IUD has higher ectopic proportion; many cases lack risks

rows.label: Clues
items: Amenorrhea, unilateral pelvic pain, spotting; cervical motion/adnexal tenderness nonspecific
★ **Syncope, shoulder-tip pain, peritoneal signs, hypotension** → hemoperitoneum/rupture
Heterotopic pregnancy possible despite visualized intrauterine pregnancy, particularly after assisted reproduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired tubal transport → extrauterine trophoblastic implantation, invasion, hemorrhage
Methotrexate inhibits folate-dependent DNA synthesis in proliferating trophoblast

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test → quantitative beta-hCG + transvaginal ultrasound**; ultrasound regardless of hCG when symptomatic
Extrauterine yolk sac/embryo diagnostic; adnexal mass/free fluid supportive; empty uterus alone insufficient
★ Stable pregnancy of unknown location → **repeat hCG in 48 hours**, serial ultrasound until resolved/localized
Discriminatory threshold up to 3,500 mIU/mL protects viable IUP; abnormal rise/fall cannot establish location

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable/rupture concern → **IV access, blood resuscitation, urgent surgery**; do not await serial hCG
Confirmed unruptured, stable, reliable follow-up, low hCG, no fetal heartbeat → consider **methotrexate**
Avoid methotrexate: viable IUP, breastfeeding, hepatic/renal disease, cytopenias, immunodeficiency, unreliable follow-up
Postmethotrexate hCG days 4/7: fall ≥15% → weekly until negative; inadequate fall → reassess/re-dose/surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, death, tubal loss, recurrence, impaired fertility
Methotrexate: mucositis, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression; rupture remains possible despite falling hCG

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat/prevent STIs, smoking cessation; prior ectopic → early ultrasound in subsequent pregnancy
Methotrexate counseling: avoid alcohol, folate supplements, intercourse until resolution; avoid conception for 3 months
Unsensitized Rh-negative ectopic → Rh(D) immune globulin; provide return precautions for escalating pain/dizziness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Miscarriage: intrauterine pregnancy loss; passage of decidual tissue alone does not prove IUP
Hemorrhagic corpus luteum: ovarian source, may coexist with normal pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt severe unilateral pain, enlarged ovary

table.title: Alternative definitive branches
rows: Stable, minimal symptoms, low declining hCG
Selected expectant management with reliable surveillance
Heartbeat, high hCG, or medical contraindication

ectopic-pregnancy.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG ectopic pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/ectopic-pregnancy), [NICE tubal ectopic management](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG126/chapter/management-of-tubal-ectopic-pregnancy); conservative discriminatory threshold established ACOG teaching.

febrile-seizures.name: Febrile seizures
febrile-seizures.scope: Simple febrile seizures, complex febrile seizures, diagnostic evaluation, antipyretics and reassurance, recurrence risk
febrile-seizures.core: Seizure during fever in a child aged 6–60 months, without CNS infection, metabolic cause, or prior afebrile seizures.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young age, family history, viral febrile illness; often occurs early in illness
Recurrence more likely with first episode <18 months, lower fever, brief preceding fever, affected relative

rows.label: Clues
items: Transient postictal sleepiness followed by return to baseline; normal neurologic examination between events
★ **Meningismus, persistent altered mental status, toxic appearance**, or focal deficit → alternate urgent diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Age-dependent neuronal excitability lowers seizure threshold during inflammatory illness
Not caused by a particular temperature rise rate; fever can be recognized only after seizure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical simple event → **clinical diagnosis; evaluate fever source**, not routine EEG or brain imaging
Bedside glucose for ongoing seizure, prolonged altered state, or concerning metabolic context
★ Suspected meningitis → **LP**; consider at 6–12 months with incomplete Hib/pneumococcal immunization
Prior antibiotics may mask meningitis; complex features prompt individualized neurologic/CNS infection evaluation
No routine electrolyte panel after brief event with normal recovery and hydration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Ongoing seizure **>5 minutes → benzodiazepine**, airway positioning, oxygen, glucose assessment
Stopped seizure, well child → reassurance, hydration, identify and treat fever source
Acetaminophen or ibuprofen improves comfort; antipyretics do not reliably prevent future febrile seizures
No chronic phenobarbital or valproate for simple events; harms exceed preventive benefit

rows.label: Complications
items: Approximately one-third recur; simple episodes do not cause intellectual disability or brain damage
Later epilepsy risk low after simple events; higher with complex features or abnormal neurodevelopment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Parent plan: **side positioning, time event, nothing in mouth**; emergency help for prolonged seizure
Selected recurrent prolonged events → home rescue intranasal midazolam or rectal diazepam plan

rows.label: Mimics
items: Meningitis: sustained encephalopathy, meningeal signs, CSF inflammation
Rigors: preserved consciousness during shivering
Epilepsy: unprovoked events outside febrile illness

febrile-seizures.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric febrile seizure evaluation principles.

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation; cholecystectomy → bile-duct injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastrointestinal-bleeding.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding
gastrointestinal-bleeding.scope: Upper GI bleeding (PUD, varices, Mallory-Weiss), lower GI bleeding (diverticular, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids), fluid and transfusion thresholds, endoscopy
gastrointestinal-bleeding.core: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia → assess hemodynamics before localizing; brisk upper bleeding can present as bright red rectal blood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NSAIDs/H pylori → ulcers; cirrhosis → varices; forceful retching → mucosal tear
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase severity; older age favors diverticula or angiodysplasia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Syncope, orthostasis, shock** signal major loss; initial hemoglobin may remain normal
Epigastric pain supports ulcer; painless bleeding favors vascular sources
Recurrent occult loss → iron deficiency; elevated BUN/creatinine ratio supports upper source

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal injury, portal-pressure collaterals, or fragile vessels rupture into GI lumen
Volume depletion → reduced perfusion; ongoing bleeding may require massive transfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type/cross, coagulation tests**, serial hemoglobin; resuscitate before procedures
Upper source → EGD within 24 hours after stabilization; suspected varices → within 12 hours
★ Ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia → **CT angiography → embolization** if active extravasation
Stable lower bleeding → bowel preparation and nonemergent colonoscopy; routine <24-hour colonoscopy adds no benefit

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crystalloid initially; stable nonischemic adults → **RBC transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL**
Active exsanguination → blood immediately regardless of hemoglobin; cardiac ischemia → individualize higher threshold
Severe life-threatening anticoagulant bleeding → drug-specific reversal; persistent bleeding after endoscopy → IR/surgery
Suspected ulcer → IV PPI; endoscopic hemostasis for active bleeding/visible vessel, then high-dose PPI

rows.label: Complications
items: Rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, AKI; variceal bleeding → infection
Massive transfusion → hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy; embolization → bowel ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H pylori and confirm cure; avoid NSAIDs; PPI for high-risk users
After variceal control: nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat banding; recurrent bleeding → TIPS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron/bismuth: dark stool without blood loss
Hemoptysis: coughing frothy blood rather than vomiting
Swallowed epistaxis: nasal source on examination

gastrointestinal-bleeding.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG lower GI bleeding 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36735555/), [ACS transfusion guidance 2025](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009).

gonococcal-infection.name: Gonococcal infection
gonococcal-infection.scope: Urethritis/cervicitis, disseminated gonococcal infection, gonococcal arthritis, neonatal conjunctivitis
gonococcal-infection.core: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes mucosal infection and can disseminate into a dermatitis-tenosynovitis-arthritis syndrome or purulent septic arthritis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: New/multiple partners, inconsistent barriers, prior STI, younger age
Complement deficiency increases dissemination risk; neonatal exposure during vaginal delivery

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, mucopurulent discharge, friable cervix; rectal/pharyngeal disease often asymptomatic
★ **Migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules** → disseminated infection
Neonate: copious purulent conjunctivitis 2–5 days after birth; corneal injury can progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci adhere to mucosa; antigenic variation permits recurrent infection
Ascending genital spread or bacteremia extends disease beyond initial exposure site

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NAAT at exposed sites**: urine/vaginal, rectal, pharyngeal; test chlamydia, HIV, syphilis
Symptomatic male urethral Gram stain may show intracellular diplococci; less reliable at other sites
Dissemination: blood/synovial cultures and mucosal NAAT; negative joint culture does not exclude diagnosis
Suspected treatment failure → culture and antimicrobial susceptibility, assess reinfection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once**; ≥150 kg → 1 g once
Chlamydia not excluded → doxycycline for 7 days; pregnancy → azithromycin instead
★ Disseminated disease → **IV/IM ceftriaxone**, hospitalization initially; drain purulent joint
Neonatal infection → systemic ceftriaxone, or cefotaxime if bilirubin/calcium concerns; topical treatment alone insufficient

rows.label: Complications
items: PID, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, epididymitis, corneal perforation
Rare endocarditis/meningitis; untreated septic arthritis damages cartilage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from preceding **60 days**; abstain 7 days after treatment and until partners treated
Retest at 3 months; pharyngeal test-of-cure at 7–14 days; routine urogenital test-of-cure unnecessary
Condoms, risk-based screening; neonatal erythromycin eye ointment prevents gonococcal ophthalmia

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chlamydia: similar urethritis/cervicitis, NAAT distinguishes
Reactive arthritis: sterile arthritis after infection, conjunctivitis/enthesitis
Staphylococcal arthritis: usually isolated hot joint without migratory skin-tendon syndrome

gout.name: Gout and crystal arthropathy
gout.scope: Acute gout, chronic gout and urate lowering, pseudogout (CPPD)
gout.core: Abrupt intensely painful inflammatory arthritis from crystal deposition; gout and CPPD require different long-term prevention despite similar flare management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gout: CKD, obesity, alcohol, purines/fructose, thiazide/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin
CPPD: older age, joint injury, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia
Flares follow surgery, dehydration, illness, or changes in urate concentration

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid-onset red swollen tender joint, often overnight; fever possible
Chronic gout: tophi on ears/olecranon, erosive arthritis; recurrent flares separated by asymptomatic intervals
CPPD in younger adults → investigate associated metabolic disorders

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Crystal phagocytosis activates inflammasome/IL-1 → neutrophilic synovitis
Most hyperuricemia reflects reduced renal urate excretion rather than excessive production

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First/atypical acute monoarthritis → **arthrocentesis**, polarized microscopy, Gram stain/culture
★ **Crystals do not exclude septic arthritis**; serum urate may be normal during gout flare
Chronic imaging: punched-out defects with overhanging edges; ultrasound double-contour sign supports urate deposition

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute either crystal flare → **NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid**; intraarticular steroid only after infection excluded
CKD/ulcer/anticoagulation → favor steroid; adjust colchicine for renal impairment/interactions; avoid NSAIDs in advanced CKD
★ Urate lowering: **allopurinol first-line**, including CKD; start low, titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL
Continue urate lowering during flares; may start during treated flare; no routine asymptomatic-hyperuricemia treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Gout: destructive arthritis, uric-acid stones; CPPD: chronic degenerative/inflammatory arthropathy
Allopurinol hypersensitivity; colchicine → diarrhea/neuromyopathy
Xanthine-oxidase inhibitors + azathioprine/6-MP → severe marrow suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Urate lowering: **tophi, joint damage, ≥2 flares/year**; first flare with CKD ≥3/stones/urate >9 → consider
Starting urate lowering → colchicine/NSAID prophylaxis 3–6 months; serial urate monitoring
Weight reduction, limit alcohol/fructose; replace thiazide with losartan when feasible; retain indicated aspirin
Before allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01 testing with Southeast Asian/African American ancestry; CPPD lacks crystal-depleting drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic arthritis: positive culture, bacteremia risk; aspiration essential when uncertain
Cellulitis: superficial inflammation, less restriction of passive joint motion
RA: persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis

gout.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACR gout guideline 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10563586/), [ACR gout education 2025](https://rheumatology.org/patients/gout); CPPD established teaching.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles, dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Start beta-blocker only when compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI requires 36-hour washout
MRA requires eGFR >30, K <5; persistent EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

heat-related-illness.name: Heat-related illness
heat-related-illness.scope: Heat exhaustion, classic and exertional heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia and NMS contrast
heat-related-illness.core: Heat exposure with neurologic dysfunction signals heat stroke, requiring immediate cooling before laboratory confirmation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Classic: older adults, heat waves, impaired sweating, anticholinergics, limited water access
Exertional: strenuous activity, poor acclimatization, heavy equipment, stimulant use

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Delirium, seizures, or coma** distinguish heat stroke from uncomplicated heat exhaustion
Tachycardia, hypotension, vomiting; sweating may persist despite severe heat injury
Core temperature often >40 °C; lower readings after cooling do not exclude heat stroke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heat production exceeds dissipation → endothelial injury, systemic inflammation, cellular dysfunction
Sweat losses → hypovolemia; excessive free water intake can produce hyponatremia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Rectal temperature**; oral, axillary, and tympanic measurements may underestimate severity
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, urinalysis, liver enzymes, coagulation studies; repeat for evolving injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, remove clothing, **rapid whole-body cooling**; do not delay for transport or tests
Exertional: cold-water immersion preferred; classic: evaporative cooling practical; stop active cooling near 39 °C
★ **IV isotonic crystalloid** for hypovolemia; benzodiazepines for seizures or shivering
Avoid antipyretics; environmental hyperthermia has no elevated hypothalamic temperature set point

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, hepatic failure, ARDS, persistent neurologic deficits
Delayed liver injury despite initial clinical improvement

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Gradual acclimatization**, scheduled rest, shade, hydration, cooling access
Avoid strenuous exercise during peak heat; monitor vulnerable adults during heat waves

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sepsis: infectious focus, fever unrelated to environmental load
Serotonin syndrome: serotonergic exposure, clonus, hyperreflexia

heat-related-illness.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency medicine teaching.

hyperglycemic-crises.name: Hyperglycemic crises
hyperglycemic-crises.core: Insulin-deficient diabetes with osmotic diuresis: rapid acidotic illness or slowly progressive hyperosmolar encephalopathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI; DKA often type 1, HHS often older type 2
Euglycemic triggers: **SGLT2 inhibitors**, pregnancy, fasting

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, dry mucosa, tachycardia
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul breathing**; HHS: profound dehydration, focal deficits
★ Severe: **hypotension, stupor**, or coma → ICU

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin deficit + counterregulatory hormones → lipolysis, ketogenesis; residual insulin in HHS limits ketosis
Total-body K depleted despite initially normal/high serum K

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, electrolytes, venous pH, β-hydroxybutyrate**, osmolality; ECG + trigger evaluation
Effective osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18; glucose in mg/dL
★ HHS: **effective osmolality >300 OR total >320 mOsm/kg**; substantial ketosis/acidosis → mixed DKA/HHS
DKA resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND (pH ≥7.3 OR HCO₃ ≥18); urine ketones/anion gap misleading

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV isotonic crystalloid → K correction → IV regular insulin**; K <3.5 mmol/L → delay insulin
Replace K when <5 mmol/L; glucose checks every 1–2 h, electrolytes/pH/ketones every 4 h
★ Add **dextrose** below glucose 250; euglycemic presentation → immediately; continue insulin until crisis resolves
SC basal insulin overlaps infusion 1–2 h; bicarbonate only consider pH <7.0; HHS: slower osmolar correction

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, thrombosis; treatment: hypoglycemia, hypokalemic arrhythmias, cerebral edema, hyperchloremic acidosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sick-day fluids/ketone checks; continue basal insulin; ensure supplies and early follow-up
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: binge then poor intake; usually no diabetes
Starvation ketosis: usually milder acidosis, no marked hyperglycemia
Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap, exposure; absent substantial ketonemia

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults may have apathetic presentation
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → radioactive iodine uptake, except pregnancy/lactation
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate, reason, communicate choice**; specific to decision, fluctuating
Competence: legal determination; diagnosis, age, or disagreement alone does not establish incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, including life-saving treatment; avoid coercion or abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no available surrogate/directive → implied consent for necessary treatment
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or substantially changed risk → renewed consent discussion

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness localizes to the ipsilateral carotid circulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: Aphasia or neglect suggests cortical involvement; crossed cranial-nerve/limb findings suggest brainstem disease
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF → oral anticoagulation with timing based on infarct/bleeding risk; high-intensity statin, BP control
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

nephrolithiasis.name: Nephrolithiasis
nephrolithiasis.scope: Renal colic, calcium oxalate, uric acid, struvite, cystine, drug-induced stones, noncontrast CT, medical expulsive therapy, surgical indications
nephrolithiasis.core: Sudden colicky flank pain radiating toward the groin with hematuria suggests a ureteral stone; infection plus obstruction is an emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low urine volume, high sodium intake, family history, obesity, gout
Hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption, recurrent urinary infection; low citrate, genetic defects

rows.label: Clues
items: Restlessness, nausea/vomiting, CVA tenderness; hematuria may be absent
★ **Fever, pyuria, hypotension, AKI, anuria** → infected or function-threatening obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Urinary supersaturation → crystal formation; obstruction raises ureteral pressure and provokes spasm

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis + culture if infection suspected**, creatinine, pregnancy test when relevant
★ Nonpregnant adult → **low-dose noncontrast CT**; pregnancy/children → renal ultrasound first
KUB misses radiolucent uric acid stones; radiographic invisibility does not exclude ureteral obstruction
Analyze passed stone; recurrent/high-risk disease → serum evaluation and 24-hour urine

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Ketorolac** for analgesia, ondansetron for nausea, normal hydration; avoid forced high-volume fluids during obstruction
Small uncomplicated stones → observation; distal 5–10 mm → consider tamsulosin
★ Infection + obstruction → **urgent stent or nephrostomy + IV antibiotics**; delay definitive stone removal
Intervene for uncontrolled pain, persistent obstruction, renal deterioration, large stone, or failed passage
Ureteroscopy/shock-wave lithotripsy selected by stone; >2 cm/staghorn → percutaneous nephrolithotomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis/urosepsis, recurrent stones, renal loss
Procedures → bleeding, infection, ureteral injury; tamsulosin → orthostasis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Aim **urine volume ≥2–2.5 L/day**, normal dietary calcium, low sodium, moderate animal protein
Recurrent calcium stones/hypercalciuria → chlorthalidone; hypocitraturia → potassium citrate
Do not restrict dietary calcium routinely; calcium with meals reduces enteric oxalate absorption

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: older patient, hemodynamic instability, aortic dilation
Pyelonephritis: fever/constant pain; torsion/ectopic pregnancy: genital/pelvic findings

table.title: Stone clues and targeted prevention
rows: Indinavir CT-occult; topiramate promotes alkaline urine

nephrolithiasis.evidence: Not checked online; established stone evaluation and prevention principles.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones, alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe constant pain, vomiting, tenderness, ileus; chronic disease adds steatorrhea and weight loss
★ **Hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria, persistent SIRS** → early monitored/ICU assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature intrapancreatic enzyme activation → autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Chronic fibrosis destroys acinar/islet tissue; lipase may normalize despite advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute diagnosis: **2 of 3**—typical pain, lipase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging
RUQ ultrasound evaluates gallstones; triglycerides, calcium, liver tests identify cause
Contrast CT for uncertain diagnosis, deterioration, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours; not routine immediately
Chronic: CT/MRCP shows calcification/duct changes; fecal elastase <200 supports exocrine insufficiency

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute: **moderate lactated Ringer resuscitation**, frequent reassessment, analgesia, electrolyte correction; avoid overload
★ **Early oral low-fat feeding** within 24–48 hours if tolerated; enteral tube feeding if unable
Biliary with cholangitis → urgent ERCP; mild gallstone disease → cholecystectomy before discharge
Sterile necrosis: no antibiotics; infected: penetrating antibiotics, delayed step-up drainage/debridement
Chronic: stop alcohol/tobacco; pancreatic enzymes, nutrition/fat-soluble vitamins, pain and diabetes management

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, AKI, shock, hypocalcemia; local necrosis, vascular thrombosis, hemorrhage
Pseudocyst after >4 weeks; infected collection, obstruction; chronic disease → pancreatic cancer and brittle diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat cause**: gallbladder removal, triglyceride control, avoid culprit drug and alcohol
Post-ERCP rectal indomethacin in eligible patients; selected pancreatic duct stenting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perforated ulcer: rigid abdomen/free air
Mesenteric ischemia: pain-exam mismatch; MI: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern

table.title: Severity and collections
rows: Transient dysfunction ≤48 hours or local complication

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent/traumatic effusion or recurrent difficult drainage → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

pneumothorax.name: Pneumothorax
pneumothorax.scope: Spontaneous pneumothorax (primary, secondary), tension pneumothorax, needle decompression, chest tube thoracostomy
pneumothorax.core: Pleural air causes acute unilateral pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds; circulatory compromise indicates tension physiology requiring immediate decompression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: tall thin young adults, smoking, family history
Secondary: COPD, cystic fibrosis, PJP, interstitial lung disease; trauma/procedures or positive-pressure ventilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Unilateral hyperresonance, dyspnea, asymmetric chest expansion; severity depends on underlying reserve
★ **Hypotension + unilateral absent breath sounds** → tension; tracheal deviation is late
Ventilated patient: sudden desaturation, rising airway pressure, hemodynamic collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of negative pleural pressure permits lung collapse
One-way air entry increases intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and causing obstructive shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable tension suspicion → **clinical diagnosis; no imaging delay**
Stable → upright chest radiograph: visceral pleural line with absent peripheral markings
Bedside ultrasound: absent sliding/B-lines supports; lung point highly specific; absent sliding alone nonspecific
CT for uncertain/complex cases; supine radiograph may show deep sulcus rather than apical air

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tension → **immediate needle or finger thoracostomy**, then chest tube; oxygen and resuscitation
Needle commonly fourth/fifth intercostal space anterior/midaxillary, or second midclavicular; insert above rib
★ Minimally symptomatic stable primary → **observation**, regardless of size, with reliable follow-up
Symptomatic/large primary → aspiration or small-bore catheter; secondary generally admit, drain if symptomatic/significant
Persistent air leak, recurrence, bilateral disease, or high-risk occupation → VATS bleb treatment/pleurodesis

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, tension progression, recurrence; reexpansion pulmonary edema after drainage
Chest tube → bleeding, infection, organ injury; blocked/clamped drain may recreate tension

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Smoking cessation**; avoid flying until radiographic resolution and clearance
Scuba diving contraindicated without specialist assessment/definitive prevention; counsel recurrence warning symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: pleuritic pain with preserved lung sliding, embolic risk
Giant bulla: intraparenchymal thin wall; CT if stable uncertainty before tube
Tamponade: shock with pericardial fluid rather than unilateral absent ventilation

pneumothorax.evidence: Conservative care checked 2026-10-30: [BTS pleural guideline 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784); tension rescue: established emergency teaching.

potassium-disorders.name: Potassium disorders
potassium-disorders.scope: Hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, cardiac membrane stabilization, shift therapy, elimination
potassium-disorders.core: Potassium abnormalities can cause weakness and fatal arrhythmias; stabilize cardiac risk while identifying the cause and correcting total-body balance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hyperkalemia: AKI/CKD, RAAS blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics, tissue lysis, insulin deficiency
Hypokalemia: GI losses, loop/thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, insulin/beta-agonists, magnesium depletion

rows.label: Clues
items: Flaccid weakness, paralysis, palpitations; symptoms may be absent despite dangerous levels
★ **K ≥6.5 mmol/L, ECG changes, or rapid rise** → emergency; normal ECG not reassuring

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extracellular K changes alter membrane excitability and cardiac conduction
Acidosis/insulin deficiency shift K outward; intracellular shifts can coexist with severe total-body depletion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG + repeat potassium**, creatinine, glucose, bicarbonate, magnesium; assess drugs and acid-base status
Hemolysis, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis → pseudohyperkalemia; repeat atraumatic draw if clinically compatible
Hypokalemia: urine K distinguishes renal wasting from extrarenal loss; interpret with BP/acid-base pattern
Do not delay treatment for confirmatory blood draw when malignant ECG changes present

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Hyperkalemic ECG toxicity → **IV calcium gluconate**; protects myocardium without removing potassium
★ Shift K inward: **IV insulin + dextrose**, nebulized albuterol; bicarbonate mainly with significant acidosis
Remove K: loop diuretic if urine output, selected binders; urgent dialysis for severe refractory/renal-failure cases
Mild/stable hypokalemia → oral KCl; <2.5, arrhythmia, paralysis, or no oral access → monitored IV replacement
★ **Correct magnesium deficiency** for refractory low K; never give IV potassium push; monitor glucose after insulin

rows.label: Complications
items: Ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, respiratory muscle failure
Overcorrection, rebound dyskalemia; insulin-induced hypoglycemia; IV potassium extravasation/phlebitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review supplements/salt substitutes; monitor K/creatinine after diuretic or RAAS-drug changes
Treat diarrhea/vomiting and underlying mineralocorticoid disorders; replace ongoing losses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: ascending areflexic weakness without explanatory electrolyte pattern
Periodic paralysis: episodic shifts, sometimes thyrotoxicosis; avoid excessive replacement causing rebound

table.title: ECG patterns
rows: Peaked T → PR prolongation → wide QRS/sine-wave
Flat T, ST depression, prominent U waves

potassium-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established electrolyte emergency principles.

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: hypotension with **bradycardia**, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
Serial lactate, capillary refill, urine output; CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway/oxygen, IV access; **balanced crystalloid**, dynamic fluid-response reassessment; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + balanced blood products**; avoid large crystalloid loads
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.name: Skin and soft tissue infections
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.scope: Cellulitis, erysipelas, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, lymphangitis, necrotizing fasciitis
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.core: Skin infection management depends on purulence, systemic illness, and signs of deep tissue destruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin breaks, tinea pedis, edema/lymphedema, diabetes, obesity, injection drug use
Prior MRSA, crowding, recent hospitalization; surgery or penetrating trauma raises deep-infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Warmth, tenderness, erythema; rapidly expanding margins or systemic toxicity require urgent reassessment
★ **Pain out of proportion**, bullae, anesthesia, crepitus, shock → necrotizing infection
Perineal involvement → Fournier gangrene; saltwater exposure → Vibrio, freshwater → Aeromonas

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonpurulent infection usually streptococcal; purulent lesions usually S aureus
Fascial spread and toxin-mediated injury → thrombosis, necrosis, sepsis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical diagnosis; **bedside ultrasound** if occult fluid collection suspected
Culture drained pus for severe, recurrent, or resistant infection; blood cultures for systemic toxicity
Suspected necrotizing disease → immediate surgical evaluation; imaging must not delay exploration
Low laboratory risk score or absent gas does not exclude necrotizing fasciitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Deep infection → **urgent debridement + vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam**, add clindamycin for toxin suppression
Confirmed group A streptococcal necrotizing infection → penicillin + clindamycin
Severe cellulitis/systemic illness → IV cefazolin; MRSA risk → vancomycin
★ Abscess: add **antibiotics** for systemic signs, immunocompromise, extensive disease, or failed drainage

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, osteomyelitis, septic thrombophlebitis; tissue loss and amputation
Toxic shock, multiorgan failure; recurrent cellulitis worsens lymphatic dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat interdigital fungal infection, manage edema, skin hygiene, protect wounds
Recurrent staphylococcal infections → consider nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine decolonization; avoid shared razors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stasis dermatitis: chronic, often bilateral, itchy
DVT: deep swelling without superficial spreading infection; contact dermatitis: pruritic exposure-pattern rash

table.title: Superficial patterns
rows: Incision and drainage; TMP-SMX if needed

venous-thromboembolism.name: Venous thromboembolism
venous-thromboembolism.core: Unilateral swollen leg or sudden unexplained dyspnea with pleuritic pain; pulmonary embolism severity determined by hemodynamics, not clot size.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Immobilization, surgery, malignancy, estrogen, pregnancy/postpartum, previous VTE, inherited thrombophilia

rows.label: Clues
items: DVT: asymmetric calf tenderness, warmth; PE: tachycardia, hypoxemia, hemoptysis, sometimes normal oxygen saturation
Syncope, elevated JVP, cool extremities → impending RV failure; normal chest radiograph does not exclude PE

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stasis/endothelial injury/hypercoagulability → venous clot; pulmonary obstruction → V/Q mismatch, RV pressure overload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Wells/pretest probability** first; very low-risk + PERC-negative → no testing
★ Low/intermediate probability → **D-dimer**; negative excludes; positive/high probability → **CT pulmonary angiography**
Age >50: D-dimer threshold age × 10 ng/mL FEU; contrast contraindication → V/Q scan
DVT → compression US; negative proximal scan + persistent suspicion → repeat in 1 week

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Oxygen/support circulation; unstable and unsafe for CT → bedside **echo**; high suspicion/delayed imaging → anticoagulate
★ Most stable VTE → **apixaban/rivaroxaban**; pregnancy → LMWH; severe renal failure → UFH
Lysis contraindicated/fails → catheter thrombectomy/surgical embolectomy; active intracranial bleeding precludes lysis
Acute proximal DVT/PE + absolute anticoagulation contraindication → temporary **IVC filter**, remove when feasible

rows.label: Complications
items: Postthrombotic syndrome; persistent dyspnea → evaluate chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
Anticoagulation/thrombolysis → bleeding; heparin → HIT

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Major transient trigger → **3 months** anticoagulation; unprovoked/persistent risk → extended course if low bleeding risk
Hospital prophylaxis: LMWH; active bleeding → intermittent pneumatic compression; early mobilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cellulitis: predominantly skin erythema, portal of entry
Ruptured Baker cyst: posterior knee symptoms, cyst on US
Pneumonia: focal infiltrate and infectious prodrome

table.title: Treatment branches; 2026 PE guidance uses categories A–E
rows: Stable; low PESI/sPESI; no RV injury
Normotensive + RV dysfunction and/or troponin elevation
Sustained SBP <90 mm Hg or shock

ventricular-arrhythmias.name: Ventricular arrhythmias
ventricular-arrhythmias.scope: Ventricular tachycardia (monomorphic, polymorphic/torsades de pointes), ventricular fibrillation, QT prolongation, antiarrhythmics, defibrillation and cardioversion, magnesium sulfate
ventricular-arrhythmias.core: Wide-complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise; pulse, stability, morphology, and QT determine immediate treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior MI/scar, cardiomyopathy, acute ischemia, channelopathies, myocarditis
Low K/Mg, bradycardia, congenital long QT; macrolides, antipsychotics, methadone, class IA/III antiarrhythmics

rows.label: Clues
items: Palpitations, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea; pulseless collapse requires immediate arrest algorithm
★ **Shock, ischemia, altered mentation, acute HF** with sustained tachycardia → unstable
Torsades often follows pause-dependent long-short sequence; recurrent self-terminating runs can precede arrest

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Scar reentry often causes monomorphic VT; prolonged repolarization produces early afterdepolarizations and torsades
VF causes chaotic ineffective ventricular activation with no meaningful cardiac output

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Check pulse immediately**, attach monitor/defibrillator; 12-lead ECG only if stabilization not delayed
AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, concordance favor VT over SVT with aberrancy
Measure baseline QTc, review drugs, electrolytes, ischemia; QTc >500 ms increases torsades risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pulseless VT/VF → **unsynchronized defibrillation + CPR**, epinephrine; refractory shocks → amiodarone/lidocaine
★ Unstable monomorphic VT with pulse → **synchronized cardioversion**; sustained polymorphic VT → unsynchronized shock
Stable monomorphic VT → IV procainamide or amiodarone; avoid procainamide with prolonged QT/severe HF
★ Recurrent torsades → **IV magnesium**, stop QT drugs, replace K; acquired pause-dependent cases → overdrive pacing
Normal-QT polymorphic VT → treat ischemia, consider lidocaine/amiodarone; magnesium not routine

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiac arrest, sudden death, hypoxic brain injury, cardiogenic shock
QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics can worsen torsades; cardioversion without synchronization can induce VF in organized rhythms

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **ICD** for survivors without reversible cause; selected low-EF patients for primary prevention after optimization
Beta-blocker for chronic ischemic/structural risk; ablation for recurrent scar-related VT/ICD shocks
Correct reversible triggers; congenital long QT needs specialist beta-blocker/ICD risk assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: SVT with aberrancy: prior bundle-branch pattern; uncertainty → treat as VT
Preexcited AF: irregular very rapid wide complexes; avoid AV nodal blockers
Artifact: palpable pulse and unaffected underlying QRS despite apparent chaotic tracing

wrist-and-hand-injuries.name: Wrist and hand injuries
wrist-and-hand-injuries.scope: Scaphoid fracture, distal radius fracture (Colles), boxer fracture, gamekeeper thumb, de Quervain tenosynovitis
wrist-and-hand-injuries.core: Mechanism and focal anatomy guide hand injury care; normal initial radiographs do not exclude a clinically important occult fracture.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fall on outstretched hand → carpal/distal radius injury; osteoporosis increases fragility-fracture risk
Closed-fist strike → fifth metacarpal; forced thumb abduction → ulnar collateral ligament injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Focal swelling, bruising, deformity, reduced grip; compare cascade and rotation with fingers flexed
★ **Numb thumb/index/middle fingers** after wrist trauma → acute median compression
Open wound, severe passive-stretch pain, pallor, or tense swelling → urgent surgical evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Carpal vascular supply and ligament stability determine ischemia/nonunion risk after injury
Displaced bone or swelling can compress nerves; rotational deformity disproportionately impairs hand function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AP/lateral/oblique radiographs**; dedicated scaphoid views for suspected occult carpal fracture
Neurovascular and tendon examination before/after reduction; document capillary refill, sensation, motor function
★ **Scaphoid suspicion despite negative films** → repeat in 10–14 days or obtain early MRI
Lateral wrist view assesses carpal alignment; thumb stress instability may require radiograph/ultrasound or MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Displacement/dislocation → **analgesia, reduction, splint**; instability/neurovascular compromise → urgent orthopedics
Thumb UCL complete tear/Stener lesion → repair; partial stable tear → thumb immobilization
Inspect knuckle wounds: fight bite → irrigation, amoxicillin-clavulanate, hand-surgery evaluation if deep
Remove rings early; open fracture → sterile dressing, IV cefazolin, tetanus assessment, urgent debridement

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ Scaphoid proximal pole → **avascular necrosis/nonunion**; missed carpal dislocation → chronic instability/arthritis
Malrotation, stiffness, tendon injury, complex regional pain syndrome; Colles fracture may cause delayed extensor rupture

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective sports equipment, fall prevention, osteoporosis evaluation after low-trauma fracture
Early finger motion when safe; splint-care counseling and reassessment for increasing pain/numbness

rows.label: Mimics
items: De Quervain tenosynovitis: radial pain with Finkelstein maneuver, no acute bony injury
Carpal tunnel syndrome: chronic nocturnal symptoms without traumatic deformity
Septic flexor tenosynovitis: fusiform digit, flexed posture, sheath tenderness, passive-extension pain

wrist-and-hand-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established hand-injury diagnosis and stabilization.
